paper_metadata.title: Dynamic High-Temperature Tensile Characterization of an Iridium Alloy
paper_metadata.journal: Dynamic Behavior of Materials, Volume 1, Conference Proceedings of the Society for Experimental Mechanics Series

evidence.section: 20.1 Introduction
evidence.quote: Iridium alloys possess unique property combinations of high melting temperature, high-temperature strength and ductility, and excellent oxidation and corrosion resistance [1–5], making them ideal for specialized applications.

evidence.section: Abstract
evidence.quote: In this study, the room-temperature Kolsky tension bar was modiﬁed to characterize a DOP-26 iridium alloy in tension at elevated strain rates and temperatures.

evidence.section: 20.3 Dynamic High-Temperature Tensile Characterization of Iridium Alloy
evidence.quote: All specimens were acid cleaned and then heat treated at 1375 ± 25 °C for 1 h ± 10 min in vacuum (1 × 10−4 Torr).

evidence.section: 20.3 Dynamic High-Temperature Tensile Characterization of Iridium Alloy
evidence.quote: The iridium tensile specimens were removed from prime DOP-26 alloy blanks using electrical discharge machining (EDM) with zinc-coated brass wire.

evidence.section: 20.3 Dynamic High-Temperature Tensile Characterization of Iridium Alloy
evidence.quote: The specimens were ground to remove the residual EDM layer, and then deburred and polished.

evidence.section: 20.3 Dynamic High-Temperature Tensile Characterization of Iridium Alloy
evidence.quote: At the 735 °C/3450 s−1 condition, the engineering failure strains varied between 0.5 and 0.7.

evidence.section: 20.3 Dynamic High-Temperature Tensile Characterization of Iridium Alloy
evidence.quote: All stress–strain curves show an initial elasticity followed by signiﬁcant work hardening behavior when the strain is below 10 %. This phenomenon may be related to a change in microstructure or deformation mechanism at high strain rates and elevated temperatures.

evidence.section: 20.3 Dynamic High-Temperature Tensile Characterization of Iridium Alloy
evidence.quote: At strains greater than 10 % and similar strain rates the ﬂow stresses decrease when the temperature increases from 750 to 1030 °C, showing signiﬁcant thermal-softening behavior.

evidence.section: 20.3 Dynamic High-Temperature Tensile Characterization of Iridium Alloy
evidence.quote: At the same temperature, the ﬂow stresses increase when the strain rate increases from ~1000 to 3500 s−1, showing a positive strain-rate sensitivity.
